outcome: No change: the largest known Woodall prime (n = 17016602, found March 2018 by PrimeGrid) remains the largest known as of September 2026; the count of known Woodall primes (34) is unchanged; Suyama's result that almost all Woodall numbers are composite (pre-2024) still stands without further progress; the infinitude question remains open with no proof, disproof, or AI involvement found.
summary: This is the classic existence/infinitude question (§3.1): 'Are there infinitely many Woodall primes?' Per the deep-dive rules, this class of question moves only when actually answered — a new example, however large, narrows nothing about whether the set is infinite. I confirmed via t5k.org's list of largest known primes, the current Wikipedia Woodall number article, MathWorld, and the PrimeGrid forum announcement that the largest known Woodall prime (of the strict form n·2^n−1) remains 17016602×2^17016602−1, found by PrimeGrid volunteer 'ScOrPIoN' (credited to Diego Bertolotti in some secondary sources) in March 2018 — before the frozen revision date and thus not a window event even if it were the kind of event that counted. No new Woodall prime (strict form) has been discovered in the 26 Jan 2024–present window; t5k.org's current top-primes list shows the 2018 discovery as still the sole strict-form Woodall prime on the list, with several 'Generalized Woodall' primes (form n·b^n−1 for other bases b, or different exponent conventions) found in 2019 and 2024 — but these are a different, related problem (a different base family), not a case of this problem, so per §3.1 they do not count as narrowing this bullet even setting aside the infinitude rule. Suyama's theorem (pre-2024, extending Hooley's method from Cullen numbers) that almost all Woodall numbers are composite is unchanged and was not revisited by any 2024–2026 work I found. I found no arXiv preprint, announcement, or lab report claiming any progress — AI-assisted or otherwise — on this specific conjecture. A search for AI mathematical achievements touching prime-counting conjectures (e.g. Axiom Math, OpenAI's twin-prime-adjacent result) turned up work on unrelated problems (twin primes in function fields), not Woodall primes. I am satisfied this is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record.
competing_reading: None found. The 'Generalized Woodall prime' discoveries (2019, 2024) could conceivably be miscategorized by a careless reader as progress on 'Woodall primes,' but they concern a materially different number family (arbitrary base b instead of base 2, and often a different exponent relationship), matching the 'related problem produced by changing the question' pattern in §3.1 rather than a restriction of it. I classify them as out of scope.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of infinitude of strict-form Woodall primes (n·2^n−1), or an authoritative source explicitly stating the open status has changed in some other way (e.g., a proof of a positive-density or zero-density result stronger than Suyama's, which would still leave the status 'open' but might warrant 'progress' rather than 'open').
